title: Searching
html:
Searching is finding where (or whether) a value lives in a collection. Linear search works on anything in O(n); binary search needs sorted data and answers in O(log n) — and the same halving trick solves a whole family of problems: first/last occurrence, counting, square roots, peaks.

Searching — given a collection and a key x, return the index of an element equal to x (or -1 / not found). The two fundamental strategies are linear search (look at every element) and binary search (halve a sorted range each step).

Linear search vs binary search

Linear searchBinary search
Requirementnone — any order, any containerdata sorted (and random access, e.g. an array)
Best caseO(1) — first elementO(1) — middle element
Average / worstO(n)O(log n)
Comparisons for n = 1,000,000up to 1,000,000at most 20
SpaceO(1)O(1) iterative · O(log n) recursive (call stack)
Works on linked lists?yesno — no O(1) jump to the middle
Use whendata is unsorted or tiny, or you search oncedata is sorted and searched many times
Key point

Sorting an unsorted array just to binary-search it once costs O(n log n) — more than the O(n) linear search. Binary search pays off when the array is already sorted or is queried repeatedly.

Linear search

Example

Input: arr = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50], x = 30
Output: 2
Input: arr = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50], x = 35
Output: -1

Idea

Walk the array from left to right and stop at the first element equal to x. Nothing is assumed about the order, so this is the only option for unsorted data.

Time O(n)Space O(1)
Key point

Every language has this built in: Python arr.index(x) / x in arr, C++ std::find, Java List.indexOf, JavaScript arr.indexOf(x) / arr.includes(x). They are all linear scans.

Binary search

Example

Input: arr = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60], x = 40
Output: 3
Input: arr = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60], x = 25
Output: -1

Idea

Because the array is sorted, comparing x with the middle element tells you which half can contain it — the other half is discarded without looking at it. Each step halves the search range, so n elements need only about log2 n steps.

1
Set the range
low = 0, high = n - 1 — the key, if present, is inside arr[low..high].
2
Look at the middle
mid = low + (high - low) // 2. If arr[mid] == x — done.
3
Discard a half
arr[mid] < x → x can only be to the right: low = mid + 1. arr[mid] > x → high = mid - 1.
4
Stop when the range is empty
low > high means no element can equal x → return -1.
Time O(log n)Space O(1)
Pitfall

mid = (low + high) / 2 overflows a 32-bit int in C++/Java when low + high > 2^31 - 1 (arrays of a billion elements — this was a real bug in the JDK for nine years). Always write low + (high - low) / 2. In JavaScript use Math.floor — / gives a fractional index.

Pitfall

Off-by-one loops. The loop condition is low <= high (not <), and the updates must be mid + 1 / mid - 1 — using low = mid can loop forever when low == high - 1.

Binary search, recursive

The same algorithm expressed with recursion: the function searches arr[low..high] and calls itself on one half. It is tail recursive — the recursive call is the last thing done — so many compilers turn it into the loop above; Python does not, and it uses one stack frame per halving.

Time O(log n)Space O(log n) call stack

Analysis of binary search

After k halvings the range has at most n / 2^k elements. The search ends when the range is empty, i.e. when n / 2^k < 1, so k ≤ log2 n + 1. Every step does one comparison (two in the worst case), which gives the recurrence and the bound below.

T(n) = T(n / 2) + Θ(1) ⇒ T(n) = Θ(log n)
CaseWhenTime
Bestx is the first middle elementΘ(1)
Averagex anywhere, or absentΘ(log n)
Worstx absent, or found on the last halvingΘ(log n) — ⌊log2 n⌋ + 1 iterations
Space (iterative)three indicesO(1)
Space (recursive)one frame per halvingO(log n)
n161,0241,000,0001,000,000,000
Max halvings (⌊log2 n⌋ + 1)5112030
Key point

The halving idea is more general than find x. Whenever a predicate is monotonic over a range — false false false true true true — binary search finds the boundary in O(log n). Every problem below is an instance of that: first/last occurrence, counting 1s, floor of a square root, peak element.

Binary search on an unsorted list

Binary search is meaningless on unsorted data: discarding a half assumes the half cannot contain x. The only ways to use it are to sort first (and then search the sorted array — the indices refer to the sorted order) or to exploit some other structure, like the slope of a mountain array below.

Example

Input: arr = [3, 6, 1, 9, 4, 2], x = 3
Output: sorted: 1 2 3 4 6 9 — index 2 in the sorted array

Time O(n log n) sort + O(log n) per querySpace O(n) for the copy
Pitfall

The index returned is a position in the sorted array, not in the original. If the caller needs original positions, sort an array of (value, index) pairs, or sort the indices by value.

Peak element in a mountain array

Example

Input: nums = [1, 2, 1, 3, 5, 6, 4]
Output: 5 (nums[5] = 6 is greater than both neighbours)
Input: nums = [1, 2, 3, 1]
Output: 2

Idea

A peak is an element not smaller than its neighbours. Binary search works without sorting because the slope at mid tells you where a peak must exist: if nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1] you are on an ascending slope, so a peak lies to the right (the array must come down eventually — or end, and the last element is then a peak). Otherwise a peak lies at mid or to its left.

Time O(log n)Space O(1)
Key point

[1, 2, 1, 3, 5, 6, 4] has two peaks (index 1 and index 5); binary search returns a peak, not necessarily the first one. Note the loop uses left < right and right = mid (not mid - 1) because mid itself may be the answer — and mid + 1 is always in range since mid < right.

Index of first occurrence in a sorted array

Example

Input: arr = [10, 10, 20, 30, 40, 40, 40, 40], x = 20
Output: 2
Input: arr = [10, 10, 20, 30, 40, 40, 40, 40], x = 40
Output: 4
Input: x = 25
Output: -1

The naive solution scans from the left and returns the first match — O(n), and the only option when the array is unsorted.

Idea

Plain binary search stops at any x. To get the first one, when arr[mid] == x check whether it is the first: it is if mid == 0 or arr[mid - 1] < x (equivalently x > arr[mid - 1]). Otherwise there are more copies to the left — keep searching the left half (high = mid - 1). The other two cases are unchanged.

1
arr[mid] < x
Search right: low = mid + 1.
2
arr[mid] > x
Search left: high = mid - 1.
3
arr[mid] == x and (mid == 0 or arr[mid - 1] != x)
This is the first occurrence → return mid.
4
arr[mid] == x otherwise
A copy exists to the left → high = mid - 1.
Time O(log n)Space O(1) iterative · O(log n) recursive
Key point

This is exactly what bisect_left (Python) and lower_bound (C++) compute — the first position whose value is ≥ x — except that they return the insertion point instead of -1 when x is absent.

Index of last occurrence in a sorted array

Example

Input: arr = [1, 2, 2, 2, 2, 3, 4, 7, 8, 8], x = 8
Output: 9
Input: arr = [1, 2, 2, 2, 2, 3, 4, 7, 8, 8], x = 2
Output: 4
Input: x = 5
Output: -1

Naive: scan the whole array and remember the last index where arr[i] == x (or scan from the right and stop at the first match) — O(n), works unsorted.

Idea

Mirror image of first occurrence: when arr[mid] == x, it is the last one if mid == n - 1 or arr[mid + 1] != x; otherwise more copies lie to the right, so continue with low = mid + 1.

Time O(log n)Space O(1) iterative · O(log n) recursive
Pitfall

Checking arr[mid + 1] before mid == n - 1 reads past the end of the array (undefined behaviour in C++, an exception in Java, undefined in JavaScript). Keep the bounds test first in the or — short-circuit evaluation then skips the access.

Count occurrences in a sorted array

Example

Input: arr = [1, 2, 2, 2, 2, 3, 4, 7, 8, 8], x = 2
Output: 4
Input: arr = [10, 20, 20, 20, 30, 30], x = 20
Output: 3
Input: x = 25
Output: 0

ApproachHowTime
NaiveLinear scan, count matchesO(n)
BetterOne binary search to find any x, then expand left and right over the copiesO(log n + k) for k copies — O(n) when every element is x
EfficientTwo binary searches: last − first + 1O(log n)
Idea

Copies of x sit in one contiguous block of a sorted array. Find the block's two ends with the first-occurrence and last-occurrence searches above; the count is last − first + 1, or 0 when first is -1. One parameterised search (find_first = true/false) does both jobs: on a match it records the index and keeps going left or right.

Time O(log n)Space O(1)
Pitfall

The original notes labelled a version with two linear scans (first from the left, last from the right) as efficient. It gives the right answer but is O(n) — no better than counting directly. Only the two binary searches reach O(log n).

Count 1's in a sorted binary array

Example

Input: arr = [1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]
Output: 2
Input: arr = [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]
Output: 7
Input: arr = [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]
Output: 0

The array is sorted in descending order — all the 1s come first, then all the 0s. The naive solution walks from the left and stops at the first 0.

Idea

This is index of last occurrence of 1, plus one. At mid: if arr[mid] == 1 and (mid is the last index or arr[mid + 1] == 0) it is the last 1 → answer mid + 1. If arr[mid] == 1 otherwise, the boundary is to the right; if arr[mid] == 0 it is to the left.

Recursive version — one call per halving:

Time O(log n)Space O(log n) call stack

Iterative version — same decisions in a loop, O(1) space:

Time O(log n)Space O(1)
Key point

If the array were sorted ascending (0 0 0 1 1), the count of 1s is n − (index of the first 1) — the first-occurrence search. Either way it is a boundary search on a monotonic sequence.

Square root (floor) by binary search

Example

Input: x = 4
Output: 2
Input: x = 10
Output: 3 (3² = 9 ≤ 10 < 16 = 4²)
Input: x = 1000000
Output: 1000

floor(sqrt(x)) is the largest integer i with i² ≤ x. The naive solution counts up from 1 until i² > x — O(√x) iterations.

Idea

The predicate mid² ≤ x is true for small mid and false for large mid — monotonic, so binary search over 1..x finds the boundary. Whenever mid² ≤ x, mid is a candidate answer: remember it and move right; otherwise move left.

Time O(log x)Space O(1)
Pitfall

mid * mid overflows a 32-bit int once mid > 46340. Use long long / long, or compare mid <= x / mid instead of squaring. Also set high = x / 2 for x ≥ 2 if you like — the root never exceeds half of x there — but the plain high = x is correct too.

Built-in search functions

LanguageLinearBinary (sorted input)Notes
Pythonx in arr, arr.index(x)bisect.bisect_left(arr, x), bisect_rightbisect_left returns the insertion point — check arr[i] == x yourself
C++std::find(b, e, x)std::binary_search (bool), std::lower_bound, std::upper_boundlower_bound = first element ≥ x; upper_bound = first > x; equal_range gives both
Javalist.indexOf(x), list.contains(x)Arrays.binarySearch(arr, x), Collections.binarySearchreturns -(insertionPoint) - 1 when absent; any index among duplicates
JavaScriptarr.indexOf(x), arr.includes(x), arr.find(fn)none — write your ownindexOf uses ===, so NaN is never found (includes handles NaN)
Pitfall

Arrays.binarySearch on [10, 10, 20, 30, 40, 40, 40, 40] with x = 40 may return 4, 5, 6 or 7 — the contract only promises some matching index. For the first or last occurrence, use the hand-written searches above (or lower_bound / bisect_left, which do guarantee the first position).

Interview Q&A

Why write mid = low + (high - low) / 2 instead of (low + high) / 2?

Both give the same value mathematically, but low + high can exceed the maximum int (2³¹ − 1) for very large arrays and wrap to a negative number, producing a negative index. low + (high - low) / 2 never computes a value larger than high. (Python integers do not overflow, but the habit is worth keeping.)

Can you binary-search a linked list?

Not usefully. The algorithm needs O(1) access to the middle element; in a linked list reaching the middle costs O(n), so the total is O(n) — no better than a linear scan. Skip lists and balanced BSTs are the pointer-based structures that give O(log n) search.

When is linear search the better choice?

When the data is unsorted and searched only once (sorting costs O(n log n)), when n is tiny (a dozen elements — the constant factors and cache behaviour favour the scan), or when the container has no random access (linked list, stream).

How do first-occurrence and lower_bound differ?

lower_bound(x) / bisect_left(x) returns the first index whose value is ≥ x — if x is absent that is the position where it would be inserted. First-occurrence returns the same index when x is present and -1 otherwise. upper_bound(x) returns the first index with value > x, so upper_bound − lower_bound is the count of x.

What problems can binary search solve besides finding a value?

Anything where a yes/no predicate is monotonic over a range: first/last occurrence, counting 1s in a sorted binary array, floor of a square root (mid² ≤ x), peak in a mountain array, the smallest capacity that ships packages within d days, the minimum page limit in allocate books — "binary search on the answer". Each step evaluates the predicate once, so the cost is O(log range × cost of predicate).

What is the worst-case number of comparisons of binary search on 1,000,000 elements?

About 20: ⌊log2 1,000,000⌋ + 1 = 20 halvings, each with at most two comparisons. Linear search needs up to 1,000,000.
